content: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) is a condition that alters the three-dimensional structure of the spine and trunk. While it is often asymptomatic, it can progress during growth, leading to cosmetic concerns. A spinal curvature exceeding 30° increases the likelihood of health complications and further curve progression in adulthood. Therapeutic exercises (TEs) are sometimes used to manage AIS, aiming to reduce curve progression and delay or avoid invasive treatments, but their effectiveness remains debated. The objective of this study was to assess the efficacy of TEs, including generic therapeutic exercises (GTE) and physiotherapeutic scoliosis-specific exercises (PSSE), in comparison to no treatment, other non-surgical interventions, or different exercise regimens. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared TEs with no treatment, non-surgical treatments like bracing or electrical stimulation, or other exercise types. Observational studies were excluded in this update due to the availability of sufficient RCTs. Thirteen RCTs involving 583 participants were included. The participants were predominantly female (50%-100%), with a mean age of 12 to 15 years, and had varying degrees of spinal curvature. The studies were assessed for methodological quality, with 61% judged to have a low risk of bias for random sequence generation and 46% for allocation concealment. However, none of the studies could blind participants or personnel, leading to a high risk of performance and detection bias for subjective outcomes. When comparing TEs to no treatment, the evidence was very uncertain regarding whether TEs reduce the Cobb angle (mean difference [MD] −3.6°, 95% confidence interval [CI] −5.6 to −1.7; 2 studies, 52 participants). Low-certainty evidence suggested that PSSE had little to no effect on the angle of trunk rotation (ATR) (MD −0.8°, 95% CI −3.8 to 2.1; 1 study, 45 participants) and may slightly reduce waist asymmetry (MD −0.5 cm, 95% CI −0.8 to −0.3; 1 study, 45 participants). PSSE appeared to have little to no impact on cosmetic issues as measured by the Spinal Appearance Questionnaire (SAQ) General (MD 0.7 points, 95% CI −0.1 to 1.4; 1 study, 16 participants) or self-image as measured by the Scoliosis Research Society-22 (SRS-22) Patient Questionnaire (MD 0.3 points, 95% CI −0.3 to 0.9; 1 study, 16 participants). However, PSSE may slightly improve quality of life (QoL) as measured by the SRS-22 Total score (MD 0.3 points, 95% CI 0.1 to 0.4; 2 studies, 61 participants). Among these, only the Cobb angle results were deemed clinically meaningful. When comparing PSSE combined with bracing to bracing alone, low-certainty evidence suggested that the addition of PSSE may reduce the Cobb angle (MD −2.2°, 95% CI −3.8 to −0.7; 2 studies, 84 participants). Similarly, GTE combined with other non-surgical interventions may reduce the Cobb angle (MD −8.0°, 95% CI −11.5 to −4.5; 1 study, 80 participants). However, the evidence was uncertain regarding whether PSSE combined with other non-surgical interventions reduced the Cobb angle (MD −7.8°, 95% CI −12.5 to −3.1; 1 study, 18 participants) or ATR (MD −8.0°, 95% CI −12.7 to −3.3; 1 study, 18 participants). PSSE combined with bracing appeared to have little to no effect on subjective cosmetic outcomes as measured by the SAQ General (MD −0.2 points, 95% CI −0.9 to 0.5; 1 study, 34 participants), self-image as measured by the SRS-22 Self-Image score (MD 0.1 points, 95% CI −0.3 to 0.5; 1 study, 34 participants), or QoL as measured by the SRS-22 Total score (MD 0.2 points, 95% CI −0.1 to 0.5; 1 study, 34 participants). None of these results were clinically meaningful. When comparing PSSE to bracing, the evidence was very uncertain regarding whether PSSE influenced the progression of the Cobb angle (MD 2.7°, 95% CI 0.3 to 5.0; 1 study, 60 participants), self-image (MD 0.1 points, 95% CI −1.0 to 1.1; 1 study, 60 participants), or QoL (MD 3.2 points, 95% CI 2.1 to 4.2; 1 study, 60 participants). None of these results were clinically meaningful. When comparing PSSE to GTE, the evidence was uncertain regarding whether PSSE had little to no effect on the Cobb angle (MD −3.0°, 95% CI −8.2 to 2.1; 4 studies, 192 participants; very low-certainty evidence). However, PSSE likely reduced ATR in a clinically meaningful way (MD −3.0°, 95% CI −3.4 to −2.5; 2 studies, 138 participants). The effect of PSSE on QoL (MD 0.26 points, 95% CI 0.11 to 0.62; 3 studies, 168 participants) and self-image (standardized mean difference [SMD] 0.77, 95% CI −0.61 to 2.14; 3 studies, 168 participants) was uncertain. Low-certainty evidence suggested that 38 out of 100 individuals receiving GTE may experience a progression of more than 5° in the Cobb angle compared to 7 out of 100 individuals receiving PSSE (risk ratio [RR] 0.19, 95% CI −0.67 to 0.52; 1 study, 110 participants). None of the included studies reported adverse effects. The authors concluded that the current evidence on the efficacy of TEs for AIS is limited due to heterogeneity, small sample sizes, and variability in comparisons. Only one study followed participants to the end of growth, showing the efficacy of PSSE over GTE, but this finding was weakened by the inclusion of studies with short-term results and unclear preparation of physiotherapists. Further RCTs are needed to strengthen the evidence and explore other clinically relevant outcomes, such as QoL, psychological and cosmetic issues, and back pain.
